explanations.D: A present pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome because tissue pressure exceeds capillary but not arterial pressure; arterial injury is also not suggested by the mechanism or the normal refill.

learning_point: Escalating pain out of proportion with pain on passive stretch under a cast is compartment syndrome or a tight cast until proven otherwise; pulses and capillary refill stay normal until late, so split the cast to skin and escalate immediately.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the junior doctor splits the cast and calls the on-call orthopaedic service in Adelaide and retrieval early, as fasciotomy cannot wait for a morning transfer; in a tertiary emergency department the registrar may be in theatre, so the ED consultant should be involved to ensure review within minutes.

generation.uncertainty_note: No Australian national guideline on compartment syndrome; the key reflects the NSW Emergency Care Institute plaster guidance and the British Orthopaedic Association standard widely used in Australian orthopaedic practice.

references.title: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation, Emergency Care Institute: Plaster and cast care; Compartment syndrome
references.locator: Recognition of a tight cast and compartment syndrome; splitting the cast

references.title: British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma (BOAST): Diagnosis and management of compartment syndrome of the limbs (2016)
references.locator: Clinical diagnosis: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch; pulses unreliable

tutor_context: Key facts: early signs are pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling and increasing analgesic requirement; paraesthesia, pallor, paralysis and pulselessness are late; management is to split cast and padding to skin, limb at heart level (not elevated above it), analgesia, urgent orthopaedic review and compartment pressure measurement or fasciotomy. Misconceptions: a palpable pulse excludes compartment syndrome; elevation high above the heart helps (it reduces perfusion pressure). Out of scope: fasciotomy technique, pressure measurement thresholds.
plan: Tests interpretation of pain out of proportion and passive stretch pain under a cast as compartment syndrome despite normal pulse and refill, evidencing 1.6, 1.4 and 1.9. Middle-aged woman re-presenting to a tertiary ED at night. Distractors: expected pain (anchoring on the simple fracture), median neuropraxia (plausible for distal radius), pulse-based reassurance (classic error). Supported by NSW ECI plaster guidance and BOAST compartment syndrome standard.

stem: You are the resident on the general ward of a large metropolitan teaching hospital. At 10:30, while taking blood from a 32-year-old man admitted with cellulitis who has a history of injecting drug use and whose hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV status are not documented, the needle slips as you withdraw it and punctures your gloved thumb, drawing blood. You still have the rest of the ward round jobs to do and the registrar is at the bedside of another patient. The hospital's occupational exposure procedure directs staff to the staff health clinic during business hours or the emergency department after hours. You completed hepatitis B vaccination at university but do not know your antibody level.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wash the puncture with soap and running water, finish the ward round jobs, then report the injury at the end of the shift

Wash the puncture with soap and running water, tell the registrar now so the ward is covered, go to the staff health clinic for risk assessment and baseline bloods, and arrange testing of the patient's blood with his informed consent
Squeeze the puncture to expel blood, apply an alcohol swab, take your own bloods on the ward and check the results tomorrow
Ask the patient's nurse to add hepatitis and HIV serology to his morning bloods without raising it with him, so you can decide whether you need treatment

explanations.A: Washing is correct but delay is not. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is most effective when started within hours (ideally within 2 and no later than 72), and the source patient's rapid testing, hepatitis B immunoglobulin decisions and incident documentation all depend on prompt reporting. Ward jobs can be handed over.
explanations.B: This follows SA Health and the ASHM national guidance: first aid, immediate reporting to the supervisor, prompt assessment by the designated service, baseline serology of the exposed worker, rapid testing of the source with consent, a risk assessment for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis and hepatitis B immunoglobulin or booster, and an incident report. The registrar covering the ward is the right person to tell.
explanations.C: Squeezing the wound is not recommended and does not reduce risk, alcohol is unnecessary, and self-ordered bloods bypass the risk assessment, counselling and the time-critical decision about prophylaxis.
explanations.D: Testing the source patient without his knowledge and consent breaches his rights. Source testing requires informed consent with a pre-test discussion; most patients agree to rapid testing when asked respectfully.

learning_point: After a needlestick, wash the wound, report immediately, attend the designated service for risk assessment and baseline bloods the same day, and arrange source testing only with the patient's informed consent.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the designated service is usually the emergency department, and HIV post-exposure prophylaxis starter packs and rapid source testing may need to be arranged through the ED or by phone with the SA infectious diseases service, which makes immediate reporting even more important.

references.title: ASHM. National guidelines for post-exposure prophylaxis after non-occupational and occupational exposure to HIV (2nd edition 2016, updated 2023)
references.locator: Occupational exposure: timing of PEP, source testing with consent, baseline testing of the exposed person

references.title: SA Health: Management of occupational exposure to blood and body fluids (Infection Control Service guideline)
references.locator: Immediate first aid, reporting and risk assessment

tutor_context: Key facts: first aid is washing with soap and water (do not squeeze, no caustic agents); report immediately; designated service performs risk assessment considering source status and exposure type; HIV PEP ideally within 2 hours and up to 72; hepatitis B management depends on vaccination and antibody status (booster or immunoglobulin); hepatitis C has no prophylaxis but needs follow-up testing; source testing requires informed consent; complete an incident report. Misconceptions: squeezing helps; the injured doctor can self-manage. Out of scope: PEP drug regimens.
plan: Tests management of a needlestick from a high-risk source, evidencing 1.6, 1.1 and 2.2. Resident on a busy metropolitan ward with competing jobs. Distractors: delay until end of shift (common real behaviour), squeeze and self-test (folk practice), covert source testing (ethical breach). Supported by ASHM national PEP guidelines and SA Health occupational exposure guidance.

stem: You are the intern in the recovery and surgical ward area of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, with the GP anaesthetist still in the building. A 78-year-old man with known benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin had an inguinal hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia this afternoon. Eight hours later he has not passed urine, is uncomfortable, and a bladder scan shows 720 mL. The nurse has attempted a 14 Fr catheter without success. You attempt a 16 Fr catheter with lignocaine lubricant gel, using aseptic technique. The catheter passes to about 20 cm with mild resistance at one point, and about 30 mL of clear urine returns. As you begin to inflate the balloon with sterile water he cries out with sharp pain in the penis, and the water is hard to inject.
lead_in: What do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Normal transient discomfort of catheterisation that should settle once the balloon is fully inflated
Bladder spasm from rapid decompression of a distended bladder
A urethral stricture that will require a suprapubic catheter
The balloon is being inflated within the urethra because the catheter tip has not fully entered the bladder

explanations.A: Balloon inflation in the bladder is painless. Sharp pain with resistance to inflation is never normal, and continuing to inflate can rupture the urethra, causing bleeding, false passage and later stricture.
explanations.B: Bladder spasm produces suprapubic cramping after drainage, not sharp penile pain synchronous with balloon inflation, and 30 mL has barely begun decompression.
explanations.C: The mild resistance was passed and urine returned, so the lumen was negotiated; a stricture presents as inability to pass the catheter. Suprapubic catheterisation is a decision for the surgeon or GP anaesthetist after failed urethral attempts, not an inference from this picture.
explanations.D: Urine can return once the tip is just past the external sphincter in the prostatic urethra, especially in a man with an enlarged prostate and a long urethra. Pain and resistance on inflation indicate the balloon is in the urethra: stop inflating, withdraw the water, advance the catheter to the hub, confirm a free flow of urine, then inflate slowly. If pain recurs or there is bleeding, stop and seek senior help, as the ANZUNS catheterisation guideline advises.

learning_point: Pain or resistance while inflating a urinary catheter balloon means the balloon is in the urethra: stop, deflate, advance to the hub and confirm urine flow before inflating.
setting_note: In a rural hospital there is no urology registrar; if the catheter still cannot be sited safely the junior doctor calls the surgeon or GP anaesthetist and may need to arrange transfer for suprapubic drainage, so recognising the error early avoids a urethral injury that would itself require transfer.

references.title: Australian and New Zealand Urological Nurses Society (ANZUNS). Catheterisation Clinical Guidelines (2021)
references.locator: Male urethral catheterisation: insertion to the hub, confirming urine flow before balloon inflation, troubleshooting pain or resistance

tutor_context: Key facts: in men insert the catheter to the hub (bifurcation) and confirm urine flow before inflating; pain or resistance on inflation means stop and deflate; after prostatic resistance a larger (16 to 18 Fr) catheter or a coude tip may pass more easily; postoperative retention after spinal anaesthesia and alpha blocker use are common; document residual volume. Misconceptions: urine return proves the tip is in the bladder; smaller catheters are always easier in BPH. Out of scope: suprapubic insertion technique, trial of void planning.
plan: Tests interpretation of pain and resistance during balloon inflation as a urethrally placed balloon, evidencing 1.6 and 1.4. Elderly man with BPH in postoperative retention at a rural hospital, intern catheterising. Distractors: normal discomfort (dangerous reassurance), bladder spasm, stricture needing suprapubic (over-reach). Supported by the ANZUNS catheterisation guidelines.

stem: On the surgical ward of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward, a 79-year-old woman who had a bowel resection 4 days ago becomes febrile to 38.6 with rigors; heart rate 104, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20. She has a peripheral cannula in her left forearm inserted 3 days ago and no central line. The registrar, by phone, asks you, the intern, to take blood cultures before the first dose of antibiotics, which the nurse is already drawing up, and to send a full blood count and electrolytes at the same time. The nurse asks how you want the cultures collected.
lead_in: Which blood culture collection technique is correct?

options.text: Two sets, each from a separate fresh venepuncture site after skin antisepsis with 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol allowed to dry, with 8 to 10 mL of blood in each bottle, taken before the antibiotics
One set drawn through the existing peripheral cannula after flushing it, to avoid a second needle in a frail patient
A single set of 2 to 3 mL in each bottle taken with the other bloods from one venepuncture, as volume matters less than speed
Two sets taken 30 minutes apart from the same venepuncture site, after the first antibiotic dose so that treatment is not delayed

explanations.A: Therapeutic Guidelines and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard recommend two sets (aerobic and anaerobic bottles) from separate venepunctures, with adequate skin antisepsis and 8 to 10 mL per bottle in adults, because yield rises with volume and two sites help distinguish contaminants from true bacteraemia. Cultures are taken before antibiotics but must not delay them by more than a few minutes; the other bloods are collected after the culture bottles from the same venepuncture.
explanations.B: Cultures drawn from an existing peripheral cannula have high contamination rates and are not recommended unless no other access is possible, and then only as one of two sets.
explanations.C: Low-volume cultures markedly reduce the chance of detecting bacteraemia; the volume inoculated is the single most important factor in yield.
explanations.D: Two sets can be taken at the same time from different sites; spacing them 30 minutes apart delays antibiotics unnecessarily, and taking cultures after antibiotics reduces yield.

learning_point: Adult blood cultures are two sets from two separate venepuncture sites, 8 to 10 mL per bottle, after chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antisepsis, before but without delaying antibiotics.
setting_note: The technique is the same in any hospital; in a regional hospital cultures may travel to a distant laboratory, so correct labelling with time and site and prompt transport matter, and the intern should ensure antibiotics are not held up waiting for a second site.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Sepsis and septic shock: investigations, blood culture collection (two sets, adequate volume, before antibiotics)

references.title: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard (2022)
references.locator: Quality statements on time-critical management: cultures before antimicrobials without delaying treatment

tutor_context: Key facts: two sets from separate sites (or one peripheral plus one from a central line if line infection suspected), 8 to 10 mL per bottle (20 mL per set) in adults, chlorhexidine-alcohol antisepsis of skin and bottle tops, inoculate aerobic bottle first with a syringe, do not draw cultures from existing peripheral cannulas, label with time and site, collect before antibiotics but never delay antibiotics in sepsis by more than minutes. Misconceptions: a single set suffices; cultures must be spaced in time. Out of scope: antibiotic selection, interpretation of contaminants.
plan: Tests recall of correct adult blood culture technique, evidencing 1.6, 1.5 and 1.1. Elderly postoperative woman with rigors on a regional surgical ward, intern instructed by phone. Distractors: cannula draw (convenience), low volume (speed), spaced sets after antibiotics (misremembered rule). Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines sepsis investigations and the ACSQHC Sepsis standard.

stem: You are a PGY2 in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital. A 31-year-old man has right iliac fossa pain, fever and a CT report of acute appendicitis. When you phone the surgical registrar with an ISBAR referral, she interrupts, calls you 'useless' for not having a lactate, says 'don't waste my time, call me when you have actually done your job' and hangs up. This is the third time this week she has spoken to you or your intern colleagues this way; one intern was in tears yesterday. The patient needs surgical admission tonight. The ED consultant is on the floor and your term supervisor, a physician, is on call for the department. Your hospital has a Director of Clinical Training and a medical education unit.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Accept that this is surgical culture, obtain the lactate and call back without comment
Confront the registrar when she next comes to the department, in front of the team, so that others see the behaviour challenged

Ask the ED consultant to escalate the referral consultant-to-consultant so the patient is admitted, then document the interaction factually and raise it with your term supervisor or the Director of Clinical Training through the hospital's process
Describe the interaction in the junior doctors' group chat so that colleagues are warned about her

explanations.A: Tolerating the behaviour harms you and your colleagues, normalises it and leaves a patient's care hostage to a registrar's mood. Good medical practice and the AMC framework expect doctors to contribute to a culture free of bullying, which includes not accepting it as normal.
explanations.B: A public confrontation escalates conflict, is unlikely to change behaviour and could itself be seen as unprofessional; the hospital has processes for exactly this situation.
explanations.C: Patient care comes first: the ED consultant can secure the admission at a senior level. Then a factual, dated note of what was said, and raising it with the term supervisor, Director of Clinical Training or medical education unit (or the hospital's complaint and support pathways), uses the graded, supported route the hospital provides. Checking on the affected intern is part of a safe workplace.
explanations.D: An informal group chat spreads the issue without resolving it, may breach confidentiality and professional standards, exposes you to allegations of defamation, and does nothing for the patient or the interns.

learning_point: When a senior colleague's behaviour is abusive, secure the patient's care through your own senior first, then document the facts and raise it through the hospital's supervision and support processes rather than retaliating or ignoring it.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the same registrar or surgeon may be the only surgical contact and the supervisor may be the director of medical services; the health network's prevocational education unit and the Rural Support Service can be contacted, and the principle of securing patient care first, then escalating formally, is unchanged.

generation.uncertainty_note: Section numbering in Good medical practice (2020) for respect for colleagues and bullying is cited from memory and should be verified; the content of the obligation is not in doubt.

references.title: Medical Board of Australia. Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia (2020)
references.locator: Section 4.2 Respect for medical colleagues and other healthcare professionals (bullying, harassment and discrimination)

references.title: AMC National Framework for Prevocational (PGY1 and PGY2) Medical Training: Outcome statements
references.locator: Outcome 2.6 Safe and supportive workplaces; Outcome 1.1 graded assertiveness and escalation

tutor_context: Key facts: bullying and harassment are breaches of Good medical practice and of SA Health workplace policy; the junior doctor's duties are to keep the patient safe (escalate the referral via their own senior), document contemporaneously, and use formal channels (term supervisor, DCT, medical education unit, Employee Assistance Program, AMA SA Doctors' Health); support colleagues who were affected. Misconceptions: it must be tolerated to get a reference; social media or group chats are a safe outlet. Out of scope: formal HR investigation processes, AHPRA notification thresholds.
plan: Tests the management of registrar bullying during a referral while keeping patient care first, evidencing 2.6, 2.1 and 2.4. PGY2 in a metropolitan ED with a consultant and supervisor available. Distractors: tolerate (common), public confrontation, group chat. Supported by Good medical practice and the AMC framework outcome statements.

stem: You are the intern on the medical ward of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward and CT only in business hours. A 56-year-old woman was admitted yesterday after a witnessed first generalised tonic-clonic seizure; her CT head and bloods are normal and she has recovered fully. She drives the local school bus. When you explain that she must not drive for the present and will need neurology follow-up, she becomes distressed: in this town everyone knows everyone, her job is the family's only income, and she asks you to 'keep this between us'. She says she will keep driving the bus because 'nothing will happen'. She has decision-making capacity. Your consultant will do a phone ward round in an hour.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Respect her confidentiality completely, document the advice not to drive and leave the decision to her
Telephone her employer to inform them she has had a seizure and must not drive the bus
Ask the ward nurse, who knows the family, to persuade her relatives to take her keys

Tell her clearly that she must not drive, document the advice, and after discussing with your consultant notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles as South Australian law requires for a driver you believe is unfit, informing her that you are doing so and disclosing nothing to her employer

explanations.A: Confidentiality is not absolute. In South Australia, section 148 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1959 places a legal duty on medical practitioners to notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles when they believe a patient is unfit to drive, and Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive sets a substantial non-driving period after a first seizure that is far longer for commercial drivers. A first seizure in a bus driver who intends to keep driving is the clearest case for this duty.
explanations.B: Disclosure to an employer is not authorised by the Act or by privacy principles; the legal pathway is notification to the Registrar, who acts on her licence. Telling the employer would be a breach of confidence.
explanations.C: Using a nurse's personal connections and involving family without the patient's consent breaches her privacy, is unprofessional and unreliable, and does not discharge the legal duty.
explanations.D: This is candid with the patient, documents the advice (which also protects the doctor), involves the senior for a decision an intern should not make alone, fulfils the statutory obligation, and limits disclosure to the minimum necessary to the authorised recipient. Austroads notes that a practitioner who notifies in good faith is protected from civil liability. Offering social work support and a clear neurology plan is part of good care.

learning_point: In South Australia doctors have a legal duty to notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles when a patient is unfit to drive; tell the patient, involve your senior, disclose only to the Registrar and document.
setting_note: In a small town the stakes for confidentiality are higher because any disclosure beyond the Registrar will spread quickly; the duty is the same in Adelaide, where the patient's anonymity is less fragile and social work and neurology are closer at hand.

generation.uncertainty_note: South Australia and the Northern Territory are the jurisdictions with mandatory reporting of unfit drivers by health professionals; the exact section (s148 Motor Vehicles Act 1959) should be verified against the current Act.

references.title: Austroads and National Transport Commission. Assessing Fitness to Drive for commercial and private vehicle drivers (2022)
references.locator: Part A: Reporting responsibilities of health professionals (mandatory reporting in SA and NT); Part B: Seizures and epilepsy, first seizure, commercial standards

references.title: Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (South Australia)
references.locator: Section 148: duty of medical practitioners to notify the Registrar of a person unfit to drive

references.title: Medical Board of Australia. Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia (2020)
references.locator: Confidentiality and privacy; disclosure required by law

tutor_context: Key facts: SA and NT have mandatory reporting of drivers believed unfit; elsewhere reporting is discretionary; the doctor tells the patient, documents, and discloses only to the licensing authority; first seizure means no private driving for a defined period (commonly 6 months if investigations normal) and much longer non-driving for commercial licences, decided with neurology; good-faith notifiers are protected. Misconceptions: the employer can be told; capacity means the patient's wish is final. Out of scope: exact non-driving periods, seizure treatment.
plan: Tests management of a confidentiality conflict with a statutory reporting duty in SA, evidencing 2.1, 1.2 and 2.4. Middle-aged bus driver on a regional ward after a first seizure, consultant by phone. Distractors: absolute confidentiality (misreads the law), telling the employer (over-disclosure), informal family pressure (unprofessional). Supported by Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, the SA Motor Vehicles Act and Good medical practice.
